item.text: The accession file is staged in the assigned Galaxy history as dataset `f9cad7b01a472135f9d6b20a879d93bc`. I have the schemas for `pysradb` and `fasterq-dump`; now I’m checking how this environment exposes Galaxy job submission so I can run those tools in that same history.
The job submission tool is available now. I’m inspecting the full `pysradb metadata` branch before launching so the submitted payload matches Galaxy’s live schema instead of guessing field names.
I’m launching `pysradb metadata` once per BioProject in the assigned history. These outputs will define the run set for the FASTQ retrieval and the required per-BioProject metadata tables.

The first submission was rejected at validation because this Galaxy wrapper expects conditional fields in flattened path form for this tool. I’m resubmitting with the exact parameter paths reported by the schema.

The `pysradb` jobs completed, but Galaxy provenance reports the tool resolved the default `search` branch even though metadata was requested. I’m inspecting the resulting datasets to see what was produced and whether it still contains enough run-level fields; if not, I’ll switch to an alternate Galaxy route.

The completed `pysradb` outputs are generic search tables with no BioProject-specific names. I need the actual table contents now, so I’m checking the configured Galaxy connection details in the environment and will use the Galaxy API only against the assigned history.

item.text: The failed branch is confirmed in the provenance: those two outputs came from an empty search query, so I’m not using them as metadata. I’m moving to the tool’s search mode with the BioProject IDs as explicit query text, which is the branch Galaxy is actually applying for this wrapper.

Purpose

\n

pysradb allows to retrieve metadata from BioProject ID or search run accession numbers and metadata, from SRA and ENA based on multiple criteria:

\n
    \n
  • BioProject ID
    • \n
  • Database: SRA or ENA
    • \n
  • Query keywords
    • \n
  • Accession number: a relevant study/experiment/sample/run accession number
    • \n
  • Organism: scientific name of the sample organism
    • \n
  • Library layout: paired or single-end reads
    • \n
  • Sample size: rounded to the nearest megabase
    • \n
  • Publication date
    • \n
  • Sequencing platform: Illumina, Nanopore or PacBio
    • \n
  • Library selection: method used to select and/or enrich the material being sequenced
    • \n
  • Library source: Type of source material that is being sequenced
    • \n
  • Library preparation strategy: sequencing technique intended for the library
    • \n
\n
\n

Outputs

\n

pysradb generates three different output types:

\n
    \n
  • Raw metadata file
    • \n
  • Statistics for the search query
    • \n
  • Graphs to illustrate the search results
    • \n
\n
\n

Sequencing instruments

\n

Comparisons between HiSeq instruments

\n

HiSeq 3000/4000 provides some improvements with respect the previous model HiSeq 2500:

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 genere up to 1.5 Tb and 5 Tb reads per run.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 use patterned flow cell technology originally developed for HiSeq X platforms.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 run 3 times faster and yield 65% more reads per lane.
    • \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 patterned flow cells contain billions of nanowells at fixed, known positions on the flow cell. The structured organization enables clustering at higher densities compared to non-pattern HiSeq designs.
    • \n
\n

However, the HiSeq 3000/4000 also have some also some limitations with respect to HiSeq 2500:

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq 3000/4000 are not recommended for low complexity sequencing. Applications such as non-unique amplicons, 16S, are currently not recommended.
    • \n
  • Libraries with low complexity within the first 25 bases of a read are not expected to produce high quality data.
    • \n
  • Library size restrictions. Libraries that are too long can result in polyclonal clusters that span more than 1 well, these will not pass filter. Smaller libraries will preferentially amplify with Illumina's new kinetic exclusion amplification so tight library distributions ranging from 300-500 bp are recommended.
    • \n
  • Very low tolerance for adapter dimers. Even as little as 1% adapter dimer can take up ~6% of sequencing reads, 10% contamination will take up 84% of reads. Illumina recommends you keep adapter contamination below 0.5% of your entire library.
    • \n
  • Higher duplication rates as compared to HiSeq 2500.
    • \n
  • Low quality read 2 (entire HiSeq 3000 install base is affected).
    • \n
\n

HiSeq 3000/4000 support DNA-seq, RNA-seq , ChIP-Seq, mate-pair, small RNA and exome library preparation. Any library preparation where there is enough sequence diversity is currently supported. Amplicon, 16S and applications with low sequencing diversity are currently not supported on the HiSeq 3000 / 4000.

\n

HiSeq 2500 is considered the most reliable model according to different sources.

\n

What type of read quality is expected from the HiSeq 3000/4000 ?

\n
    \n
  • 2 x 50bp \u226585% bases > Q30
    • \n
  • 2 x 75bp \u226580% bases > Q30
    • \n
  • 2 x 150bp \u226575% of bases >Q30
    • \n
\n

What is the difference between MiSeq and HiSeq?

\n

HiSeq and MiSeq platforms are among the most widely used platform to study microbial communities. But the two platforms differ in the length and amount of reads.\nMiSeq can run 600 cycles to produce 200 million 300 bp reads, on the other hand, HiSeq 2500 can run 500 cycles to produce 120 million 250 bp.

\n

What are the differences between HiSeq and NovaSeq?

\n

The Illumina NovaSeq provides a massive upgrade in sequencing throughput compared to the HiSeq 4000. There are more stringent library requirements and requires a\nlarger sample size. Due to the vast amount of data produced by the NovaSeq and the known issue of index swapping, unique dual-indexed libraries are required.

\n

What are the characteristics of HiSeq X instruments?

\n
    \n
  • HiSeq X is recommended for whole genome sequencing only (including whole bisulfite sequencing). This means that it is not adequate for RNA-seq, exome, ChIP-seq or small RNA-seq applications.
    • \n
  • Plant and animal samples can be sequenced on the HiSeq X.
    • \n
  • Expect coverate is over 30x or approximately 375 million reads per lane by loading one sample per lane.
    • \n
  • Hiseq X Ten generates utilize 2x150 base pair read configurations and has slightly better GC coverage than the HiSeq 2500.
    • \n
\n

What are the differences between MiSeq and Nextseq?

\n

The NextSeq Series of systems delivers the power of high-throughput sequencing with the simplicity of a desktop sequencer. NextSeq instruments represent an improvement when compared with Miseq, despite generating sorter reads (150bp, compared to MiSeq 250bp). NextSeq is recommended in\nthe following applications & methods:

\n
    \n
  • Exome & large panel sequencing (enrichment-based)
    • \n
  • Single-cell profiling (scRNA-Seq, scDNA-Seq, oligo tagging assays)
    • \n
  • Transcriptome sequencing (total RNA-Seq, mRNA-Seq, gene expression profiling)
    • \n
  • Methylation sequencing
    • \n
  • Metagenomic profiling (shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics)
    • \n
  • Cell-free sequencing & liquid biopsy analysis
    • \n
\n

Regarding the maximum number of reads per ran, MiSeq can generate 25 million, vs 400 million generated by the Nextseq 550 instrument. MiSeq recommended for sequencing samples of low diversity.

\n

What are the differences between HiSeq and NextSeq?

\n

The main technical difference between HiSeq and NextSeq will be the number of dyes each machines use. HiSeq uses traditional color coding with four different dyes, while NextSeq uses two dyes. This does not give any practical differences in terms of the data quality, but the trend in illumina sequencers are more into the direction of reducing the number of dyes.

\n

What is the difference between Nextseq and NovaSeq?

\n

The NovaSeq 6000 system offers deep and broad coverage and is recommended for large whole-genome sequencing (human, plant, animal) projects. It generates 250 bp reads,\nwith 20 billion maximum reads per run. NovaSeq 6000 instruments have not application based restrictions.

\n

Illumina maximum read-length summary

\n
    \n
  • MiSeq: between 300 and 600 bp
    • \n
  • NextSeq: 300 bp
    • \n
  • HiSeq 2500: between 250 and 500 bp (depending of the sofware)
    • \n
  • HiSeq 4000: 150 bp
    • \n
  • HiSeq X: 150 bp
    • \n
\n

Nanopore models - single-molecule ultra-long-read sequencing

\n

Nanopore sequencing provides the longest read lengths, from 500 bp to the current record of 2.3 Mb, with 10-30-kb genomic libraries being common. Even after error correction, sequencing error rates of corrected nanopore reads (1.5-9%) are still higher than those of corrected PacBio reads (<1%).

\n

PacBio SMRT instruments - single-molecule long-read low-error rate sequencing

\n

PacBio Sequel II CLR sequencing represents a major advancement in sequencing throughput over previous PacBio platforms with the production of more sequencing data and longer reads versus RS II and the Sequel I.\nThe PacBio HiFi sequencing method yields highly accurate long-read sequencing datasets with read lengths averaging 10-25 kb and accuracies greater than 99.5%.

inhibitors (NAIs) and cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitors (CENIs) represent two classes of antiviral drugs recommended for early treatment of patients with seasonal influenza A virus (IAV) infections. However, only limited human data, particularly on combination antiviral treatment, are available to inform optimal dosing regimens against novel IAVs, including highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus, associated with severe disease. Clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses have caused outbreaks in avian and mammalian species worldwide, highlighting the need to assess antiviral drug efficacy against these strains. We challenged ferrets with a D1.1 genotype A(H5N1) virus and treated infected animals with the NAI oseltamivir phosphate (OST) and the CENI baloxavir acid (BXA), alone or in combination, with treatment onset commencing pre- or post-symptom onset (24- or 48-hours post-inoculation (p.i.), respectively). When administered pre- or post-illness onset, BXA, but not OST, monotherapy provided significant reduction of clinical signs and significantly decreased infectious viral levels (in both respiratory and extrapulmonary specimens) compared with mock-treated animals. Combination OST/BXA treatment, when administered pre- or post-symptom onset, resulted in significant improvements in both metrics versus OST monotherapy. infections. However, only limited human data, particularly on combination antiviral treatment, are available to inform optimal dosing regimens against novel IAVs, including highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) virus, associated with severe disease. Clade 2.3.4.4b A(H5N1) viruses have caused outbreaks in avian and mammalian species worldwide, highlighting the need to assess antiviral drug efficacy against these strains. We challenged ferrets with a D1.1 genotype A(H5N1) virus and treated infected animals with the NAI oseltamivir phosphate (OST) and the CENI baloxavir acid (BXA), alone or in combination, with treatment onset commencing pre- or post-symptom onset (24- or 48-hours post-inoculation (p.i.), respectively). item.text: I’m transforming the Galaxy metadata into the required per-BioProject tables with explicit normalized column names, then writing a manifest that points only to the downloaded FASTQ files under `reads/`.

item.command:
/usr/bin/bash -lc "python3 - <<'PY'
import csv
from pathlib import Path

base = Path('/workspace')
meta_dir = base / 'final_answer' / 'metadata'
reads_dir = base / 'final_answer' / 'reads'
trace = base / 'run_trace'
meta_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
reads_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

projects = {
    'PRJNA1354216': trace / 'downloaded_metadata' / 'PRJNA1354216.pysradb.tsv',
    'PRJNA1339024': trace / 'downloaded_metadata' / 'PRJNA1339024.pysradb.tsv',
}
required = [
    'bioproject', 'run_accession', 'study_accession', 'experiment_accession',
    'sample_accession', 'biosample', 'organism_taxid', 'organism_name',
    'library_strategy', 'library_source', 'library_selection', 'library_layout',
    'instrument_model', 'run_total_spots', 'run_total_bases',
]
manifest_rows = []
summary = []

for bioproject, path in projects.items():
    rows = []
    with path.open(newline='') as fh:
        reader = csv.DictReader(fh, delimiter='\\t')
        for row in reader:
            # pysradb search returns current public records; keep only rows explicitly linked to the queried BioProject.
            linked = any(row.get(k, '') == bioproject for k in ('study_external_id_1', 'study_alias')) or bioproject in '\\t'.join(row.values())
            if not linked:
                raise SystemExit(f'row for {row.get(\"run_1_accession\")} is not linked to {bioproject}')
            is_public = row.get('run_1_is_public', '').strip().lower()
            if is_public and is_public not in {'true', '1'}:
                continue
            layout = row.get('library_layout', '').strip().upper()
            run = row.get('run_1_accession', '').strip()
            if not run:
                raise SystemExit(f'missing run accession in {path}')
            out = {
                'bioproject': bioproject,
                'run_accession': run,
                'study_accession': row.get('study_accession', ''),
                'experiment_accession': row.get('experiment_accession', ''),
                'sample_accession': row.get('sample_accession', ''),
                'biosample': row.get('pool_external_id') or row.get('sample_external_id_1', ''),
                'organism_taxid': row.get('sample_taxon_id', ''),
                'organism_name': row.get('sample_scientific_name', ''),
                'library_strategy': row.get('experiment_library_strategy', ''),
                'library_source': row.get('experiment_library_source', ''),
                'library_selection': row.get('experiment_library_selection', ''),
                'library_layout': layout,
                'instrument_model': row.get('experiment_instrument_model', ''),
                'run_total_spots': row.get('run_1_total_spots', ''),
                'run_total_bases': row.get('run_1_total_bases', ''),
            }
            rows.append(out)
            if layout == 'PAIRED':
                fwd = f'reads/{run}_1.fastq.gz'
                rev = f'reads/{run}_2.fastq.gz'
                if not (reads_dir / f'{run}_1.fastq.gz').is_file() or not (reads_dir / f'{run}_2.fastq.gz').is_file():
                    raise SystemExit(f'missing paired FASTQ files for {run}')
            elif layout == 'SINGLE':
                fwd = f'reads/{run}.fastq.gz'
                rev = ''
                if not (reads_dir / f'{run}.fastq.gz').is_file():
                    raise SystemExit(f'missing single FASTQ file for {run}')
            else:
                raise SystemExit(f'unexpected library_layout for {run}: {layout"'!r}'"')
            manifest_rows.append({
                'bioproject': bioproject,
                'run_accession': run,
                'library_layout': layout,
                'forward_path': fwd,
                'reverse_path': rev,
            })
    seen = set()
    for r in rows:
        if r['run_accession'] in seen:
            raise SystemExit(f'duplicate run in {bioproject}: {r[\"run_accession\"]}')
        seen.add(r['run_accession'])
    with (meta_dir / f'{bioproject}.tsv').open('w', newline='') as fh:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=required, delimiter='\\t', lineterminator='\\n')
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)
    summary.append((bioproject, len(rows), rows[0]['library_layout'] if rows else ''))

manifest_rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r['bioproject'], r['run_accession']))
if len({r['run_accession'] for r in manifest_rows}) "'!= len(manifest_rows):
    raise SystemExit('"'duplicate run accession in manifest')
with (base / 'final_answer' / 'run_manifest.tsv').open('w', newline='') as fh:
    fieldnames = ['bioproject', 'run_accession', 'library_layout', 'forward_path', 'reverse_path']
    writer = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=fieldnames, delimiter='\\t', lineterminator='\\n')
    writer.writeheader()
    writer.writerows(manifest_rows)

with (trace / 'execution_log.tsv').open('w', newline='') as fh:
    writer = csv.writer(fh, delimiter='\\t', lineterminator='\\n')
    writer.writerow(['step', 'detail'])
    writer.writerow(['assigned_history', 'bbd44e69cb8906b5444e24b360c0b4b9'])
    writer.writerow(['input_bioprojects', ','.join(projects)])
    writer.writerow(['metadata_tool', 'pysradb search 2.5.1+galaxy0; verbosity 3; one query per BioProject'])
    writer.writerow(['read_tool', 'fasterq-dump 3.1.1+galaxy1; --split-3; skip_technical=true; input all_sra_runs.txt'])
    for bioproject, count, layout in summary:
        writer.writerow([f'{bioproject}_runs', f'{count} rows; {layout}'])
    writer.writerow(['fastq_files', f'{len(list(reads_dir.glob(\"*.fastq.gz\")))} downloaded Galaxy datasets'])
